"A single moon universally appears in all waters; all the moons in the waters are subsumed within that one moon.
This saying is heard by many, yet those who truly understand it are few. If one were to understand it, one would know that Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva manifests many bodies from a single body.

Pleasure and aversion, good and evil, beauty and ugliness, are like echoes in a valley or flowers in a mirror; though one seeks their form and characteristics, they cannot be found at all.

Therefore it is said that although all sentient beings are saved, in reality there are no beings saved. Nevertheless, what can be done for those of the six realms of extreme suffering who are shrouded by the net of ignorance?

Alas! This Bodhisattva’s great kindness, great compassion, great filial piety, great vows, and great majestic spiritual power are all inconceivable.

To begin with, just as the hundred rivers flow until they reach their limit in the sea, so does the perfect fruit of the One Vehicle accord with the nature of reality to pervade the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

The *Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow Sūtra*, translated by Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Tang dynasty, employs a style of language that is concise yet its meaning is profound.

For this reason, the assembly at the Radiant Light (Prabhāsa) praised it as being of the world.

Yet, this cause and effect are perfectly integrated, with the principal and the retinue mutually interpenetrating.

Their mutual penetration is such that even the Buddha-eye finds its profundity difficult to fathom, and the Sage’s mind cannot measure its subtlety. Thus one knows that when the mind is unobstructed, a pure land is not distant;

Thus, those wandering on the path of delusion shall joyfully encounter royal banquets during times of famine, and those within the blazing fires of the burning house shall suddenly obtain refreshing coolness. Preface to the Annotated Commentary on the Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Sūtra of His Original Vow:

The *Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Sūtra of His Original Vow* is the swift path for sudden liberation from birth and death, the bridge for reaching Nirvana with speed, the excellent medicine for reviving the dead and returning them to life, and the precious mirror for closing off evil and promoting goodness. Furthermore, by means of...

Is it not this very sutra alone that enables one to uproot the seeds of doubt with the hand of faith, ascend to the blissful lands with the feet of precepts, and perfect immeasurable merit through the eye of wisdom and the concentrated mind?
Therefore, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is truly the fundamental field of merit upon which all sentient beings rely.
If one can take refuge in and revere this Bodhisattva, then all sufferings will be entirely eliminated.
All vows fulfilled, one attains peace and security in the present and will certainly achieve liberation in the future.
If one invokes his great name or it merely passes through the ears, grave offenses are forever extinguished and one ultimately reaches the precious fruit.

All of this is brought about by the power of the Great Being’s inconceivable compassion and vows; that mountain of compassion and ocean of vows truly surpasses those of all other great bodhisattvas. Thus it was said.
The kalpas [of merit] are doubled; therefore, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, together with the assembly of devas and humans, entrusted this Great Being and further praised him, saying:
"In the mere snap of a finger, those who take refuge in Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva shall immediately attain liberation from the retribution of the three evil realms.
To begin with, the Buddha-dharma is vast and its practices are immeasurable; all such meritorious deeds—
Among all virtues, the generation of the bodhicitta and the arousal of vows are the most essential.

Reflecting deeply upon the Bodhisattva’s past lives as the son of a householder and as the maiden Guangmu, he generated the mind and aroused vows to cultivate the six pāramitās in equal measure, thereby perfectly realizing the three bodies and becoming fully endowed with merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Consequently, his name is now proclaimed throughout the ten directions, and his emanations pervade the myriad worlds to deliver beings extensively.
All sentient beings arise through the generation of the great mind and the arousal of great vows; thus we know that the generation of the mind is the very root of all vows.

No merit whatsoever arises apart from this. Nevertheless, these originally possessed great vows arise from the essence of wisdom, while the vast oaths of deliverance are born from the function of compassion.
From the initial generation of the mind until the final attainment of the Way, they lead and guide all practice.
The aspiration for the fruit of enlightenment is its foundation; therefore, nothing precedes the vow in the attainment of Buddhahood.
It is said that without aspiration, many fall back—like an ox without a driver, like a painting without glue, or like unbaked clay that can never be used. Thus, a sutra says:
"O Bhikṣus, one who does not make a vow shall ultimately not attain the Way of the Buddha. The merit of such a vow is beyond measure; it leads to the ultimate goal.

This is the place where ambrosia is extinguished. I have often deeply contemplated this sutra and examined it with care; its essential core consists of compassion, filial piety, and the practice of vows. Why is this?
It is because the maiden Guangmu possessed a heart of great compassion and made a great vow on behalf of her mother.

Thus, compassion can give rise to filial piety, and through filial piety one gives rise to vows; from these vows, practice arises. When these are opened forth, they constitute compassion, filial piety, vows, and practice.

Taken together, these constitute the *Compassionate Vows*. Recently, the Dharma Master Yunxia from China sent me a copy of his annotated commentary on the *Sūtra of the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva* (Dizang pusa benyuan jing), which he had compiled himself, to the Reverend Yuefeng of Higashi-Hongan-ji in Kyoto.
This master, Reverend Yuefeng, was a fellow provincial with Dharma Master Yun. I have heard that Dharma Master Yun composed this commentary while ill; it consists of six fascicles in total.
How easy is it to speak of such merit! This sutra has been in existence for over a thousand years since the Tang dynasty, yet only now have there been those to provide commentaries upon it;
alas, this may indeed be called difficult. This is truly due to the Bodhisattva’s protective mindfulness and the good vows of the Dharma Master;
once the demonic afflictions had receded, his valor was unsurpassed. The Buddha spoke of "valor," and its name is Kṣitigarbha. Thus, was not the Dharma Master Yuncha [indeed one of such valor]?
"Are you not one who is capable of harmonizing with the Buddha’s intent? I wish to request that this commentary be carved into woodblocks and circulated throughout the world.
Master Yue assented and handed it over to me. I was overcome with joy, as if I had obtained a rare treasure.

Now that it has been entrusted to the press, I universally pray that all who see or hear it may come to know the matters concerning the fundamental vows, merits, and benefits of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, thereby planting the seeds of wisdom for the future.

Furthermore, seeing the fruit and fearing the cause, one ceases evil and exerts oneself in good; casting away delusion to return to the truth, one looks up with faith to receive and uphold [this teaching].
Like swallowing a diamond, it certainly cannot be digested, yet one will ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Because this inconceivable and honored sutra is truly a compassionate bounty for all sentient beings, its moistening of all things is inexhaustible. To encounter such a wondrous scripture after many kalpas is a blessing greater than this.
Therefore, disregarding my own ignorance and meanness, I have composed this preface.

This is because the profound slander of those who do not recognize the depth of their own debt of gratitude is countered by exalting the fundamental principle of the Way through kinship.

This was precisely to demonstrate the great filial piety that transcends the mundane; does this not reside within our Śākya clan? Yet, it was necessary to wait for the opportune moment to emit radiance and assemble the divisions [of the assembly].

Because the Great Being, during his causal stage, was born as the Brahmin girl and the girl Prabhāvatī, and in both instances initiated the *saṃnāha* (armor of resolve) for the sake of saving his mothers—his heart being in perfect resonance with that of our Buddha—this Sūtra of the Original Vow of Kṣitigarbha was preached. First, it clarifies the principal agent of transformation—namely, the Great Being who manifests in the hells (*niraya*) as the master who converts through filial conduct and causes beings to be reborn in the human and celestial realms.
Second, it clarifies the objects of transformation—the class of offenders who are unfilial toward their two parents and the Triple Gem, who commit evil and fall into suffering. Third, it clarifies...
Regarding the conditions for deliverance, one should immediately have them read the sutras on filial piety and make offerings to the image of the Great Filial One;

Having attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he first established the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa.

To be filial toward one's parents and respectful toward one's teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem—is this not the practice of filial piety? Is it not the orthodox core of this single sutra? The preface is written to elucidate this.

The *Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Sūtra of Fundamental Vows* weaves together the original source:
fundamentally, the self-nature of a single thought is profoundly still and tranquil; the mind of this self-nature is inherently empty and luminous.
Without form and without name, it transcends all thought and discussion. It serves as the refuge for all living beings and the root-source of all phenomena. Ultimately...

It is designated as the Middle Way and True Emptiness; it is praised and extolled as the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). When the Buddhas awaken to it, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are perfectly manifested;

when sentient beings are deluded regarding it, they circulate through the six realms of existence. Although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, there is no difference in the nature of the mind.
Thus, an ancient master said: "Pointing to the world of empty space, it is all my own mind; examining the retribution for good and evil..."
All these are but delusions of the mind. Since the fundamental single mind permeates all phenomena, the gateway to my Buddha-dharma takes the mind alone as the Way.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates;
within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind. The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the root of faith in the Mahāyāna."
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas—all of which are intended by this meaning.
This is precisely what the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha stated: "All dharmas arise from the mind."
They form characteristics together with the mind; they exist through conjunction, arising and ceasing together, and likewise lack any abiding.

Since all objective spheres merely follow what the mind takes as its object and continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment, they are able to be maintained as existing for a temporary duration.
This is precisely why I am pointing toward this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. For now, let us set aside the matter of awakening and discuss only delusion.
Among devas, humans, and asuras, they ascend lightly by following wholesome qualities; among those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, they sink downward due to evil karma.
Within those who sink as hungry ghosts and animals, there is a distinction between light and heavy, yet when one sinks into the hells, there is no difference of great or small.
This is distinct. It is entirely due to the distortions of ignorance that the very gates of hell come into being.
Thus we know that ordinary beings, because they are oblivious to the source of the mind, follow deluded thoughts; they falsely create evil karma and falsely undergo the retribution of suffering.

Were it not for the great compassion of the Most Holy One, how could the extreme agony of this inverted suspension be resolved? For this reason, the Compassionate King Kṣitigarbha has directed his focus specifically toward the realm of the netherworld.
Internally, through compassion of the same essence, he has provided rescue and aid across kalpa after kalpa without ceasing.
Śākyamuni Buddha specifically ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to repay the kindness and virtue of his Holy Mother;

he repeatedly and earnestly entrusted her with instructions, commanding that she offer even a small amount of water or flowers within the Buddha-dharma so that both might be liberated from the sufferings of the dark paths and be able to behold [the Buddha] for even a single moment before the Great Being.

In this rite, all have received the joy of this sublime site; its merit is beyond measure, and its significance is unfathomable. Although I was born in this degenerate age, I have fortunately encountered the True Vehicle (Saddharma).
Thus, I have cultivated a heart of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and utilized this place as a bridge for crossing over. I hereby briefly set forth my humble observations.

This brief explanation of the title seeks the secret empowerment of the Triple Gem to synthesize and integrate all texts. It is my universal aspiration that all who see or hear this may together proceed to the Land of Bliss.
Now, first, I shall provide a general explanation of the title; second, I shall present the contemplative method as a whole;

I. Explaining the Names; II. Discerning the Substance; III. Clarifying the Thesis; IV. Discussing the Function; V. Judging the Characteristics of the Teaching.
The reason for providing these five preliminary explanations is that the meanings within this sutra are profound and subtle;

they enable a person to comprehend the names upon a single glance, recognize the substance expressed by those names, understand that to manifest this substance one must clarify the essential thesis, realize that once the thesis is established the substance is revealed, and finally attain the power of its wondrous function. Thereafter...
If one judges this to belong to the teachings of the *Shimi-bu* (Section on the Flavor of Time), then its meaning and intent become clear and cool, manifest before the eyes and mind.

Now, it takes the inconceivable person and phenomena as its name, the inconceivable nature and consciousness as its essence, and the inconceivable practices and vows as its central tenet. The inconceivable...
The provisional means (*upāya*) are taken as the function; the revelation of the unsurpassed *amṛta* (ghee) is taken as the characteristic of the teaching. Regarding the explanation of the title:

in the six characters of "The Original Vow of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva," these constitute the specific title, as they distinguish this scripture from others. The single character "Sūtra" is the general title, as it applies to other scriptures as well.
Furthermore, the specific title is divided into person and dharma: "Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva" is the person, and "Original Vow" is the dharma. This is the original [explanation].
The Buddha himself established three titles for this sutra: first, "The Original Vow of Kṣitigarbha"; second, "The Original Practice of Kṣitigarbha";

and third, "The Sutra on the Power of Kṣitigarbha’s Original Vow. Here, only the single title "Original Vow" is highlighted because the vow necessarily entails practice, and once that practice is perfected, there must inevitably be the power to grant rescue and extraction;
therefore, by citing the title "Original Vow," the remaining aspects are naturally and effortlessly encompassed.
Second, regarding personal names, there are both general and specific designations. "Kṣitigarbha" (Earth Store) is the specific name; "Bodhisattva" is the general designation.
According to the *Buddhabhāṣita-aṣṭamahābodhisattvamandala-sūtra*, the name Kṣitigarbha should be transcribed as *Kṣitigarbha* (pronounced with the *kṣa* as a conjunct).
Its meaning is translated as "Earth Store. If one follows various other translations, it should be stated as *Ghusa* (for Earth), *Kuśa*, *Vika*, or *Caka*.

*Ka* (迦) is translated as "to store" (*kṣaya*). A sutra states: "Just as all sentient beings rely upon the earth as their single, uninterrupted support"—this is how the name is established based on a metaphor.
Now, the earth is fundamentally a single substance, yet that which it stores is immeasurable.

This is because it is the foremost of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), occupies the center among the five phases (*pañca-dhātu*), is produced from the primordial vital energy (*yuanqi*), and is the progenitor of the myriad things. Its trigram is *Kun*, and its virtue is called "the Mother. [This concludes the section on] Zhou.

The *Yi* says: "How supreme is the primal source of Kun! All things derive their life from it. It contains all with vastness and radiance; all categories of beings flourish therein. Its essence and function are broad and profound;
its virtue is so great that it is difficult to name. Thus, it is able to sustain, nourish, support, and give birth [to all]. This is an explanation according to the Confucian scriptures.

If one follows the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) to explain the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*), it is said: "From the first stage onward, it possesses the power to abide, maintain, grow, and produce."
The meaning of "bearing the burden" (荷負) reaches its ultimate fulfillment later on, and it likewise possesses three meanings. This refers to the ground (*bhūmi*) in terms of its nature (*dhātu*):

through the cultivation of the myriad practices (*sādhana*), the myriad virtues (*guṇa*) are perfected in the fruit, all of which possess these three meanings. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"In whatever place sentient beings may be, if they plant various seeds in either fallow fields or fertile fields, whether they diligently attend to their labors or do not attend to them..."

Regarding future sentient beings, he entrusted them to the celestial palaces to deliver and liberate. Just as the great earth is that upon which all rely for support, growth, and sustenance, the sutra says:
"The mind is like the great earth; it can settle all things. For this reason, the Buddha stated that the power of the mind is great;

in all these cases, the earth is used as a metaphor to clarify the nature of the mind. As for the term "Treasury" (garbha), it is also established based on a metaphor, precisely because in the world...
The seven-jeweled treasuries within the interim are analogous to the secret treasury of the three supramundane virtues. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"It is like a person who possesses seven treasures but does not bring them out for external use; this is called a 'treasury' (qùshēng).

The reason such a person stores and accumulates these treasures is for the sake of the future—namely, when grain is expensive, when bandits invade the country, or when encountering a wicked king, so as to use them to ransom one's life or for other purposes. (Cái)

It is only when a rare opportunity arises that it should be brought forth for use; the secret treasury of all Buddhas is likewise so. Thus, Zhan’an said: "It is called 'secret' (mi) because it is hidden;
it is called a 'treasury' (zàng) because it is covered. Because sentient beings do not understand it, it is termed 'esoteric' (mìbì).

The Dharma-realm encompasses and contains all phenomena; its utility is inexhaustible, and thus it is named a 'treasury. This is because sentient beings inherently possess the jewels of the three thousand [realms]."

Obscured by the six thieves of affliction and slain by the evil king of the mental consciousness, one must bring forth this secret treasury of the three virtues to ransom the life of the permanent abiding [nature].
It is precisely for this reason that the name "Kṣitigarbha" (Earth-Treasury) is taken.
This secret treasury of the three virtues is enshrined within the bodies and minds of all sentient beings; the Buddhas awaken to it and thereby realize it, while sentient beings remain deluded by it.
Thus they transmigrate; yet this secret treasury has never been altered from the beginning.

Therefore, from the first moment Kṣitigarbha-sattva generated the *saṃnāha* (vow of armor) until his abiding in equal enlightenment, his own practice and his transformation of others have never departed from this secret treasury of the mind.

This secret treasury of the mind is itself *nirvāṇa*. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The Bodhisattva’s initial resolve is to constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path;

this is the initial cultivation for one's own practice (*svārtha*). It also causes sentient beings to constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa*; this is the initial cultivation for the practice of transforming others (*parārtha*).
To place all children within the secret treasury is the subsequent entry [into the Path] through the transformation of others. I, too, shall before long abide therein myself."
This refers to entering [the path] after one has practiced for oneself. Thus we know that from the initial mind of both self and others, there is none who does not practice;

and from the subsequent minds of both self and others, there is none who does not enter. Now, based on this principle, I shall briefly explain its name. The Sanskrit name is *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which in Chinese is translated as "Great Extinction and Deliverance" (*dà mièdù*).
"Great" (*dà*) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "extinction" (*miè*) refers to liberation (*vimukti*); and "deliverance" (*dù*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Within these three dharmas—
Each and every one is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, they are called "virtues.

These four virtues are not separate from my own mind, and those four treasuries do not transcend the earth. It is like when Maitreya attains Buddhahood: in his land, there will be a Wheel-Turning King.

It is named Śaṅkha (the first character is pronounced as *rǎng* [level tone], and the second as *qū*; it is also written as *Shuāngqū*, which translates as "conch shell," specifically a *śaṅkha* shell; the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* calls it Saṃgha). It resides in the city of Ketumatī.
When Maitreya attains Buddhahood, four great treasuries of jewels will simultaneously manifest.
Each of these great treasuries is surrounded by four hundred million smaller treasuries. The great treasury of *Ibhadra* (a treasury of gold) is located in Gandhāra.
The *Ratnākara* Great Treasury (Silver Treasury) is in the country of Mithilā; the *Piṅgala* Great Treasury (Moon-Bright Pearl Treasury) is in the country of Surāṣṭra;
and the *Śaṅkha* Great Treasury (Lapis Lazuli Treasury, also named Conch-Shell Treasury) is at the Mountain of the Ancient Seers in Vārāṇasī.
These four treasuries are all located within the land of Jambudvīpa; likewise, these four virtues are now fully present within the ālayavijñāna.

Gold is a metaphor for the virtue of permanence (*nitya*), because its color does not change. Silver is a metaphor for the virtue of bliss (*sukha*), because it gladdens the human heart. The bright pearl is a metaphor for the virtue of self (*ātman*), because the manifestation of forms is sovereign.
Lapis lazuli is a metaphor for the virtue of purity (*śubha*), because it is transparent both internally and externally. Furthermore, one should know this.
When these four treasuries had not yet been revealed, each was secretly protected by nāgas and spirits who guarded them so they were not lost.
Once they were opened and developed, there were no guardians; when people saw them, their minds felt no attachment. This is a precise metaphor for the treasure-trove of the mind-ground.
Although it remains hidden and yet undiminished during times of delusion, it is realized and yet not clung to at the very moment of awakening.

Thus, one knows that the mind-treasury is fully endowed with all jewels—namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—which accord with every aspiration. The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are three things without distinction.
The meaning of the name "Kṣitigarbha" (Earth Store) is as follows. Thus, in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbhasūtra*, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Subhāṣtapraśna:
"O Great Being, you have accomplished such inconceivable dharmas of merit. You are a treasury of these various supreme merits;
you are the source from which the jewels of all liberations emerge. Why is this so? Because you are the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."
They bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, fulfilling their aspirations like a wish-fulfilling jewel and like a hidden treasure.
Such a Great Being, desiring to bring sentient beings to spiritual maturity, has long cultivated firm great vows and great compassion.
His courageous diligence surpasses that of all other bodhisattvas; therefore, you all should make offerings to him.

Now, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, our Buddha has earnestly entrusted the sentient beings of the dharma realm to Kṣitigarbha, commanding that all beings from this Sahā world until the appearance of Maitreya be brought to liberation and forever freed from all suffering, so that they may encounter the Buddhas and receive [their prophecy].

"Journalist" (記者): This is because [the Buddha] intends to reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), thereby placing the great jewels of the four virtues entirely within the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
"Bodhisattva": In full, it should be called *bodhisattva*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "Bodhi" refers to the path of the Buddha;
"sattva" refers to one who brings sentient beings to fulfillment. One is able to seek supreme enlightenment (*bodhi*) above through wisdom, and to [save] those below through compassion.
"Saving sentient beings. Tiantai says: "Because one employs the path of all Buddhas to bring sentient beings to fulfillment, one is called a Bodhisattva (菩提薩埵).
However, the name 'Bodhisattva' should encompass the four teachings; now that [the truth] has been revealed and clarified, it specifically points to the Perfect Teaching (圓教).

Furthermore, by prefixing this general name with 'Earth Store' (地藏), although it remains general, it nevertheless retains its specific character. Next, he explains the dharma of the original vow. "Original" refers to the fundamental...
In the past, "Brahma" was named *Nidhi*; in this land, it is translated as "Vow" (*Praṇidhāna*), signifying a longing, desire, or aspiration, and a term for the pursuit of fulfillment.
This refers to the great vows originally made by the Bodhisattva when he was born as the Brahmin girl and the girl Guangmu.
It is also his fundamental nature; for the Bodhisattva relies upon the ground of his original nature to exalt the root of his vows. As it is said:

Gazing upward at the Great Awakened One, who has spent countless kalpas delivering sentient beings without ever succumbing to weariness or fatigue, it is because he has fulfilled the vows of his original ground.

Furthermore, this is the power and function of one’s own fundamental nature. When a Mahāsattva establishes vows based on that original ground, they give rise to faith within their own mind and, in turn, place their trust in their own mind.
This is like a tree that takes root according to the soil; when the roots are deep and the foundation is vast, the branches and leaves flourish in dependence upon them.
Flourishing flowers and fruits grow lush from this; though the fierce winds be great, they cannot shake it. To wish that which does not rely on the Truths is called a "wild wish.
For the Truths to not follow the mind is termed "deviant truth. Now, take the mind as the ground and the Truths as the roots.

The vow is the root; thereafter, the branches of correct practice flourish, the leaves of the aids to enlightenment grow lush, and the flowers of the seven factors of awakening and the fruit of the eightfold noble path ripen.
Thus, one forms a tree within the forest of the Dharma and adorns the grove of dhāraṇīs. Therefore, one must invoke the root by establishing a vow;
only then can the mind be firmly restrained, so that even when encountering the winds of external objects, it cannot be thwarted or destroyed. This proceeds from the root.

This is the general outline of establishing vows. However, there are both general and specific aspects. The general aspect refers to the Four Great Vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*). As stated in the *Beichan wen* (The Text for the Great Compassion Repentance):

"Now, as for the Four Great Vows, they arise based upon the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). Regarding the Four Noble Truths: first, they demonstrate the causes and effects of suffering in the mundane world;
second, they demonstrate the causes and effects of happiness in the supramundane realm. All Bodhisattvas desire to uproot this suffering and bestow this happiness; therefore, they rely upon them."
He established the four vows. Based on the Truth of Suffering, he said: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. Based on the Truth of Origination, he said:
"Afflictions are innumerable; I vow to sever them all. Based on the Truth of the Path, he said: "Dharma-gates are inexhaustible; I vow to know them all."
It is established based on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). It is called "universal" because all Bodhisattvas together resolve: "I vow to attain the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
However, in the *Saptabuddhaka-sūtra*, there are instances of four vows, eight vows, twelve vows, as well as the forty-eight vows of Amitābha and the sixteen vows of Avalokiteśvara;
these are specific to individual persons and are therefore called "particular. If one follows the present sutra:
The Brahmin girl and the girl Guangmu both resolved their minds for the sake of their mothers to rescue those in the six realms;
thus, filial conduct constitutes the specific vow of these Great Beings at the time of their initial resolve. Furthermore, this is also the fundamental vow made by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Both the general and the specific are embraced together. Collectively, the Four Great Vows constitute the root of this aspiration, which is never-failing in its manifestation.

Specifically, it is through the heart of compassion that one directs oneself toward those sentient beings undergoing suffering, vowing to eternally serve as the Teacher for the dark realms. Thus, whether general or specific, both arise from the fundamental nature.
Although they are distinguished as general and specific, there is not one that does not aim to uproot the causes and effects of worldly suffering and to bestow supramundane bliss.
Regarding cause and effect, one must diligently distinguish between the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect. Siming said:

"Furthermore, one must understand that the characteristics of the beginning and the end are such that their essence and nature are fused and identical. Jingxi said: "From the very first thought, all is universally encompassed; one contemplates afflictions as the Dharma-realm.

To realize afflictions as wisdom and birth as extinction is called the 'Perfect Four Vows. Therefore, by understanding the former two vows, one uproots the suffering of inherent virtue; [the latter...]"

Second is the vow: to bestow the bliss of inherent virtue. Since suffering and bliss are inherent to their nature, what need is there to extract or bestow them? This is the vow of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Now, in the distant past, across countless kalpas, the Great Being Kṣitigarbha made a great vow to shoulder the burden of sentient beings of the six realms who suffer from transgressions, teaching them to uphold the True Dharma and giving rise to all merit; he endured suffering and overcame hardships.
Because of his great kindness and great compassion, he is named Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow. This concludes the explanation of the specific name.

As for "sūtra" (jīng), it is the general designation for the holy teachings; with the exception of the Vinaya and Śāstras, all such works receive this title. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), its Sanskrit name is *sūtra*.

Some say there is no equivalent translation, because it possesses five meanings: "containing a gushing spring" (for its meaning is profound and inexhaustible), "giving birth" (for it can produce sublime goodness), "a carpenter’s line" (for it establishes the correct and the deviant), "manifesting" (for it reveals the capacity for what is right), and "stringing a garland" (for it threads together all dharmas). Thus, it is left untranslated due to its multiple connotations.

Some say there are translations: translations of sutras, translations of śāstras, translations of the *dharmamūla*, translations of *sūtra* (threads), and translations of the teachings of virtuous speech.
These are all translations based on their meanings. Tiantai, for now, relies upon one name as the standard so as not to cause resentment between the two schools.

From antiquity to the present, when transcribing from Sanskrit into Chinese, they have all been titled "Sutras" (*jing*). This is because, in this land, the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are referred to as the "Five Classics."
Although various scriptures are individually titled simply as "sūtras," all treatises refer to them as *sūtra* (契經).

This means that they accord with the principle of the two truths above and accord with the capacities of the three faculties below. Furthermore, the terms are interpreted as "constant" (*nitya*) and "dharma," each possessing three meanings. That which cannot be altered by Māras or heretics is called the constancy of teaching;
that which is authentic and unmixed is called the constancy of practice; and that which is tranquil and immovable is called the constancy of principle. As for dharma, it can...

"Gui" (軌) means that conduct is to be followed as a model and principle is to be followed as a model. If the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains it as "penetrating and upholding," this is intended in the sense of using thread to string together a garland.

Cien (Ci'en) says: "To be constant and to be the Dharma; this is to gather and to string together, so that all may emerge from the ford of suffering and ultimately return to the shore of enlightenment.
In this way, regarding these two aspects of person and Dharma, there are two layers of both general and specific meanings, skillfully borrowing from the subtle.
Regarding the title: it is established according to its name; thus, it is called the *Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Sūtra on Fundamental Vows*.
Second, concerning the explanation that inconceivable nature-consciousness constitutes the essence, this is established based on three points. First, by relying upon the sūtras and śāstras.
2. The Root of Delusion and Enlightenment. 3. The Fundamental Consciousness of Bodhisattvas. The Sūtra states:

"The fundamental consciousness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*) of all sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation is indeterminate; whether it gives rise to good or evil depends on its following of external objects. It further states:

"When the name of a Buddha or Bodhisattva reaches the ear-organ of a person at the moment of death, it may be heard and enter their fundamental consciousness. This consciousness refers specifically to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
Therefore, the *Vairocana-samādhi-dharmaparyāya* and the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, in the section on the Heart of the Lotus Family, both state:
"What is this mind? It is the seeds of the habitual tendencies of affliction; both good and evil arise from the mind; the mind is the ālayavijñāna. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: because it relies upon the Tathāgatagarbha, there is a mind that arises and ceases; that which is called 'neither arising nor ceasing'..."

It is in union with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different; this is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Thus, it takes the coexistence of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature as its cause—is this not so?
Paramārtha translates it according to the name as "the consciousness that does not perish" (*amūla-vijñāna*), taking the sense of "not losing.

Xuanzang translates it according to the meaning as the "store-consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), because it is able to contain and store the seeds of all phenomena. Indeed, such is the essence of this consciousness.
It is called an "ālaya" (storehouse) because it possesses three qualities: being that which can store, that which is stored within, and that which is clung to as a store.

Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "The eighth fundamental consciousness is vast and boundless; it reveals the source of the mind as having no exterior and encompasses the nature-store in its universal penetration.

It holds the title of 'retainer of seeds' and acts as the sovereign of total retribution. It establishes the substance of sentient beings and stands as the cause for nirvāṇa. Based on this, [the name] is established.
As for its substance, it encompasses all phenomena; one might say it is like grasping the collar of a garment or pulling the main cord of a net.
Regarding the source of delusion and enlightenment, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "This is based on the ālayavijñāna, wherein it is said that ignorance exists, arising from non-enlightenment."

Because it can see, can manifest, and can apprehend objects, this consciousness is called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*), as it serves as the support for all knowable phenomena, whether defiled or pure.
It is also called the "seed-consciousness" (*bījavi-jñāna*), because it universally sustains the seeds of all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
This is precisely what Vimalakīrti meant when he said: "From the root of non-abiding, all phenomena are established."
Jingxi’s commentary states: Ignorance serves as the basis for all phenomena (*dharmas*). Ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*);
ignorance, in turn, takes the dharma-nature as its basis. One should know that all phenomena likewise take the dharma-nature as their basis.
The dharma-nature is itself ignorance; the dharma-nature, moreover, takes ignorance as its basis. The dharma-nature is itself ignorance; the dharma-nature has no place of abiding.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Ignorance has no place of abiding. Although both ignorance and the dharma-nature are without abiding, they act as the foundation for all phenomena.
Thus, while being without abiding and without marks, the phenomenal and the principle are eternally equal;

yet they establish the distinctions between awakening and delusion regarding all phenomena. Therefore, the *Sūtra on Examining the Grounds* states: "From beginningless time, it has coexisted with the mind of ignorance."
Due to the power of the habitual perfuming of the causes and conditions of deluded darkness, false objects appear.

Because of the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming of these false objects, a mind associated with delusion arises, reckoning "self" and "what belongs to self," thereby accumulating various karmas and undergoing the suffering of birth and death;
such a state of the Dharma-body is called a "sentient being. If, within such sentient beings, the habitual perfuming of the Dharma-body accumulates and becomes powerful...
When their afflictions gradually thin out, they are able to feel weary of the world and seek the path to nirvāṇa;
with faith they take refuge in the single reality and practice the six pāramitās and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Such a person is called a bodhisattva.
If, among such bodhisattvas, one fully cultivates all wholesome dharmas and ultimately succeeds in awakening from the sleep of ignorance, they are renamed a Buddha. It should be understood that...
One should know that these categories—sentient beings, bodhisattvas, buddhas, and so forth—exist as distinctions only by virtue of worldly conventional designations and names.
However, the essence of the *dharmakāya* is ultimately equal, devoid of any marks of difference.

Therefore, one should know that if one does not penetrate the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) endowed with these virtues, one must instead take the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as the object of focus to sever the cultivated defilements and cultivated evils of the nine realms. Why is this?
It is called "inconceivable. Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "This consciousness establishes the sentient and the insentient, and gives rise to defiled and pure dharmas.
If there is knowing and perceiving, then the realm of sentient beings arises; if there is no thought and no deliberation, then the lands arise through conditions.
Due to defiled dharmas, one revolves through the six destinies; following pure dharmas, one ascends the four stages of the noble ones. This is indeed so.

This refers to the foundation of both ordinary beings and sages, and the source of their spiritual capacities. If one thoroughly understands the origin of this consciousness, what dharma would not be awakening?
If one realizes this nature of mind, what realm would not be true? It may be called the gate of transcending study and the dwelling-place for the settling of the spirit;

thus, this essence is established as the root-source of delusion and awakening, thereby manifesting how the Great Being disperses shadows and divides forms within realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, throughout the sea of birth and death.
Guiding them according to their capacity, one uproots the source and dries up the fountainhead, turning delusion into awakening.

This is precisely because the essence of this non-arising, non-perishing Dharma-nature resides right within the midst of arising-and-ceasing ignorance and false conceptualization. Thus, Nanyue said: "The source of the Way is not far;
the ocean of nature is not distant. Seek it only within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere. This is exactly what that means. As for the term "Bodhisattva":
Regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*): the *Guangming xuanyi* states that the *ālayavijñāna* is precisely the eighth, the non-extinguishing consciousness.

Because it still possesses latent afflictions (*anuśaya*—so called because they "sleep" within the continuity [of existence]), when distinguished separately, it is the consciousness of a bodhisattva. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says, when it resides in the mind of a bodhisattva, it is termed *prajñā*;
this is its meaning. Indeed, this consciousness serves as the superior basis for a bodhisattva’s vision of the Buddha.

This is the basis of marks. Because the Tathāgata’s sublime physical marks are all equal in measure to empty space, they are perceived through the karmic consciousness and observed with intermediate wisdom.
For this reason, Kṣitigarbha, within the Tuṣita Heaven palace, unites his manifested bodies to behold the Buddha.

It is precisely by relying on this fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Furthermore, this consciousness serves as the source from which the Middle Way gives rise to transformations in accordance with conditions.

This refers to the fact that while icchantikas do not sever their inherent virtuous nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), when they encounter conditions, that virtue is skillfully activated; likewise, Buddhas do not sever their inherent evil nature, and thus transform beings by sharing in their evil.
Now, the Great Being Kṣitigarbha thoroughly understands the matter of the cultivated evil of icchantikas and others, such that his entire being is [identical to it].
This is the principle of the inherent evil of nature: even extremes and heterodoxy are none other than the Middle Way; the five heinous crimes are liberation in their very place.

The Universal Manifestation Body (Sambhogakāya) wanders and transforms throughout the various realms of existence, pointing out this source of delusion so that beings may know equality. It is precisely by relying on this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that all great transformations arise.
This is what is designated as the *ālayavijñāna* when abiding in the initial stage, but which is called simply "Non-existence" (*Amala*) when situated in the stage of fruition.

It is free from defilement, fully encompasses the stages of wisdom in both their fundamental and subsequent aspects, and establishes the gateway to benefiting both oneself and others. How could its merit be slight?
Because these three meanings are present, the inconceivable nature-consciousness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*) is established as the true essence (*dharmatā*) of this sutra.

Question: Some masters claim that the nature-consciousness belongs to the realm of phenomena (*dharma*) and thus cannot serve as the essence; rather, one must point to the principle (*li*) of the nature of consciousness as being the true meaning of "essence. This must necessarily be so.
This means that if one establishes this "nature" based on the consciousness (vijñāna) according to the sūtras, it would be a nature of false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

How could one rely upon such a thing to establish the essence of the sūtra? These words are indeed highly appropriate. If you, Master, certainly do not accept this, then whose teaching shall we follow?

Answer: The indication of the "nature of consciousness" has a basis in its meaning; the establishment of "consciousness-nature" has its textual authority. As for our current interpretation, it is as follows: [The text continues with the specific analysis].

The *Mohe zhiguan* states that both the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) serve as the fundamental basis. This has already been cited and need not be discussed further. It is simply as the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* clarifies regarding the two truths:

"One merely identifies the dharma-nature as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) arising from ignorance as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)."

How could this conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) not be a phenomenon? This is precisely a phenomenon that is identical with principle (*tattva*). Since it is named the "poisonous nature of principle" (*li-dōng-xìng-è*), it is also termed "nature-defiled following conditions" (*xìng-rǎn-suí-yuán*).
Thus, the *Shìqiān* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua Xuanyi*) states: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the beginning of delusion regarding the truth;

the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) points entirely toward ignorance. From time immemorial, how has it ever not been the truth? Conventionally, there are the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses; truly, they co-reside.
One must know that because they share the same nature, they are able to coexist within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

This is what is meant by the *Fuxing* [Commentary]: "The three thousand [realms] do not transcend the dharma-nature of a single thought-moment; the three thousand do not transcend the ignorance of a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, there are two ways this school explains the passage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding "the mind creating [all things]": first, from the perspective of principle (*li*), "creating" means "possessing"; second, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), it refers to...

The transformations and constructions of the three periods of time, and so forth, all arise only through the inherent presence of principle (*li*), which then gives rise to phenomenal function (*shi*).

Thus, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) relies upon the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) to manifest the defiled dharmas of the six realms. Establishing this "nature-consciousness" (*xing-shi*) as the essence is precisely for the sake of those with sharp faculties, so that they may reveal the principle directly within phenomena.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature. Ignorance and...
Affection (*tṛṣṇā*). This middle between the two is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). However, while principle (*li*) has no fixed location, it is omnipresent within phenomena (*shi*).

Now, since phenomena are entirely identical to principle, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself the nature (*prakṛti*). Why then do you not allow that [consciousness] can be established as the essence? Therefore, one knows that both the nature of consciousness and consciousness itself can serve as the essence.
It is simply that, for the time being, we establish this doctrine from the perspective of the *ālayavijñāna* regarding its side of delusion, taking ignorance (*avidyā*) as the root.
This interpretation accords with the sūtras and śāstras, and thus does not contradict the instructions of our patriarchs.

However, if one were to point to the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as being a false, habitual nature (*vāsanā*), this view may not yet be entirely correct. Why is this so? Because a false, habitual nature is invariably indeterminate.

Now, why further question the lack of fixity? Since this has already been identified as false and delusive, then the nature of the lack of fixity in the underlying will and character is likewise false and delusive.
If it is a delusive nature, what is the use of applying one’s will? One must know that this nature is precisely the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
Since the *dharmatā* is shrouded by ignorance, its entire substance belongs to the realm of delusion; thus it is called "delusive consciousness. How could this not be the Truth?

Is this not the meaning of "following conditions"? Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) quotes the *Guanwuliangshoujing* (Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Infinite Life): "The essence and characteristics of ignorance are fundamentally non-existent;
they exist only through the conjunction of deluded thoughts and conditions. They are produced by the mental activities of improper reflection.
It is like a magician at a crossroads who conjures various elephants, horses, necklaces, people, and other things; the ignorant take these to be real, while the wise [know them to be empty]."

Know that these are not real. Through the illusion of ignorance, the six realms and their environments and inhabitants are manifested; one should know that they are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.

Because they are produced by ignorance, they are called the "distinctions of the six realms. They are not created by Īśvara or other such agents; they all emerge from the single thought-moment of the ignorant mind.
Therefore, this is established as the essence (*tattva*). It directly corrects former delusions and brings about present awakening.

To realize that the cultivation of defilement and the cultivation of evil are themselves the *pratyaya-bhāva* and *jñāna-bhāva* Buddha-natures, and thus to "return home by way of the path," is called the "inconceivable.

Hence, we know that it is by taking the nature-consciousness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*) as the essence that the six realms of existence are enabled to break the shell of ignorance and achieve the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). Thus, in my "General Demonstration," I said:
For now, let us set aside the discussion of awakening and address only the matter of delusion;
this is the intended meaning. Third, regarding the clarification that the inconceivable practice and vows constitute the central theme:

according to the sutra, Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha, "What practices did the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha perform in his causal stage, and what vows did he establish, such that he was able to accomplish inconceivable deeds? Furthermore...
In the past, incalculable eons ago, this Bodhisattva was the son of a great elder.
Having beheld the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita, who was adorned with the marks and signs of perfection and endowed with the ten thousand practices, he asked that Buddha:

"By what conduct and vows did you attain these physical characteristics? Furthermore, the Tathāgata himself composed the name of this sūtra; it is called "The Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha," and it is also called "Kṣitigarbha."
This concerns fundamental practice (*caryā*). Therefore, one should know that the two dharmas of practice and aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) constitute the essential core of this sutra.

The explanation of aspiration is as previously stated. Regarding "practice" (*caryā*): the Sanskrit term is *caryā*, which in this [Chinese] context means "practice. As for why these two dharmas must necessarily be established as a pair, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:

"The practices and deeds of all bodhisattvas are pure, and they thus naturally obtain pure retribution. Why, then, is it necessary to establish an aspiration before obtaining them? It is like a field..."
"If one's household obtains grain, why would one need to wait for a prayer? [The Master] replied: "If one performs meritorious deeds without making a vow, there is nothing established.
A vow acts as a guide and leader, enabling things to be accomplished. Now, the task of adorning the Buddha-field is a great matter; it cannot be accomplished by practicing merit alone."
It must rely upon the power of vows. For example, although the strength of an ox can pull a cart, it requires a driver to reach a destination.
It is the same with the vow for a pure world. Furthermore, the bodhisattvas of the four teachings each have two types of vows: the general and the specific;

their bestowal of happiness is not without distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. The inferior vow brings about the causes and conditions for happiness in this life; the middling vow [brings about happiness] in future lives.
The causes and conditions for worldly happiness; and the supreme vow for the causes and conditions for the bliss of nirvāṇa.

Now, as this is the teaching that reveals and clarifies the ultimate truth, I establish my vow with a resolute mind, relying solely upon the Unsurpassed One Vehicle (Ekayāna), so that all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm may together attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Since the aspiration has been thus formulated, so too must the practices be undertaken. Although the aspects of practice are manifold, to cite them briefly, there are three dharmas: morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the ladder for transcending the world and the standard protocol of the Buddha-dharma. In their middle mode, they are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*);

as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, these are taught for those seeking the path of a bodhisattva, who "should fulfill the six pāramitās to cross the flow of birth and death and ascend to the shore of nirvāṇa. In their extensive mode, [they are...]
The myriad practices, even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When a bodhisattva practices *prajñā*, although they know that all phenomena have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), they are also able to know the manifold characteristics (*nānālakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Now, these various phenomena are collectively subsumed and returned to a single verse.
An ancient worthy said: "To observe the manifestation in the world, one extensively explains the grid-patterns of the myriad practices;

yet to contemplate what accords with the principle, one only chants the essential framework of four lines. The *Śīla-sūtra* says: "Commit no evil, practice all that is good, and purify your own mind."

"This is the teaching of all Buddhas. The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) explains: "All evils" refers to the transgressions and offenses of the sevenfold course of action, whether minor or grave, and whether they constitute violations or not;

such evils are what the precepts prevent. "All virtues" refers to the three virtuous courses of action—whether in a state of distraction or stillness, including the preparatory stages (*pūrvāpara-prayoga*) and the auxiliary merits (*aṅga-vana-guṇa*).
Since these are all pure and ascending, they are termed "virtuous. Regarding "purifying one's own mind," it destroys all... [text fragment ends].

Perverse inversion. To thoroughly understand the causal and auxiliary dharma-gates of the mundane and supramundane, which can remove the defilements of the mind and purify all blemishes—how could anything surpass wisdom?
The vast ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entirely encompassed by these three.

However, because the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ, and because one must respond to them according to their needs, the manifestations of practice vary. This distinguishes the capacities and natures, as well as the divisions between those who rely on faith and those who rely on the Dharma.

Zhiyi distinguishes between the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) practices by enumerating their differences. Here, I shall first clarify the Separate practice as the provisional designation for the Perfect. The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to explain five types of practice:
First, the Holy Practice (*āryacaryā*), which refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom; these serve as the causes for one’s own cultivation. Second, the Brahma Practice (*brahmacaryā*).

These are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). These constitute the practice for transforming others while on the causal stage (these two being the causal practices cultivated prior to the stages).

Third, the Celestial Practice (*devacaryā*): this refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and above. Having realized the ultimate truth of the celestial realm—the natural principle—one acts in accordance with that principle;

thus it is called the Celestial Practice (this practice pertains to the dwelling within the stages). Fourth, the Infant Practice (*bālacaryā*): this refers to manifesting the same practices as those cultivated by the three vehicles and the seven preparatory expedients (*saptaprayoga*). Fifth, the Illness... [text ends]

Regarding "conduct": this refers to manifesting a physical form identical to that of the nine realms and the three obstacles (both of these are forms of responsive activity arising from the fruit; when appearing identical to those on the side of wholesome birth, it is called "infant-like conduct," arising from the root of great kindness;
when appearing identical to those on the side of afflictions, it is called "sickly conduct," arising from the root of great compassion).

Now, when the Great Being Kṣitigarbha sees sentient beings breaking the precepts and committing offenses, thereby losing the happiness of humans and devas as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa, he knows the origin of suffering (*samudaya*). He wanders through birth and death, experiencing the miserable realms.

"Retribution" is precisely the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha*). When the accumulation of suffering (*samudaya*) is in opposition to morality, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*), there is no Path (*mārga*).

Because there is no Path, one does not attain *nirvāṇa*; thus, there is no cessation (*nirodha*). Desiring to uproot the accumulation of suffering, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and establishes two vows.
Desiring to extinguish desire through the Way, one gives rise to great compassion and establishes two vows.

Having made these vows, one then practices the three trainings and the six perfections, along with various aspirations and deeds, to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the Buddha-lands. Now, practice is called "advancing forward," yet it cannot proceed without wisdom.
Wisdom and understanding guide practice; without them, the objective is not rectified. With wisdom as the eyes and practice as the feet, one reaches the state of cool serenity.
The pond is the source from which these practices are understood. Practice can bring wisdom to fruition; thus, when practice is perfected, wisdom becomes complete.
Wisdom can manifest principle; when principle is fully realized, wisdom ceases. If these were merely to depend upon one another in this way, they would not constitute wondrous practice.

Now, the Great Being directly realizes that cultivated evil is itself inherent evil. Because inherent evil is interfused, it spontaneously encompasses the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm, thereby illuminating all transgressions.

All phenomena are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*). The ten evils, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the eight heterodoxies are all dharma-gates of the poison of principle;
they are entirely the fundamental functions of the defilement of nature. By means of these wondrous practices, one teaches and transforms all sentient beings.

Understanding this consciousness of nature as the essence of the objects illuminated and manifested, and employing this wisdom-practice as the wondrous principle that illuminates and manifests, one first takes the real as the object.

The marks [of phenomena] are such that as they encounter objects, they are immediately the Middle Way; there is nothing that is not true reality. One’s own realm, the Buddha-realm, and the realm of sentient beings are likewise so.
The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness (*tathatā*); there is no suffering to be abandoned. Ignorance and worldly afflictions are themselves bodhi;

there is no accumulation to be severed. Extremes and heterodoxy are all the central correctness; there is no path to be cultivated. Birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa; there is no extinction to be realized. It is purely and solely reality.
Marks. There is no separate dharma apart from this; it is further a single practice called the Tathāgata-practice, which is the one practice that encompasses all practices.
Thus, by using wisdom to illumine the object and using the object to give rise to wisdom, one contemplates the true reality of karma and perceives the source of transgression.

The dharmatā and ignorance mutually integrate and dissolve into one another. Is it not the case that all that observes is the threefold contemplation within the one mind, and all that is observed is the three?

The truths are one in their single object; though one, they are discussed as three, and though three, they are discussed as one. Object, wisdom, and practice—these three are equally termed the "Secret Treasury.
They are like the three eyes of a celestial king, or like the three dots of the letter *ī*. Whether one or three, none are lacking or diminished.
Thus, the essence is the essence of the school, and the school is the school of the essence. Therefore, inconceivable practice and vow constitute the school’s tenet.
The fourth treatise concerns the inconceivable application of skillful means. According to the sutra, the Buddha addressed Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, saying:

"In this world of five turbidities, I teach and transform sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce, causing their minds to be subdued. I manifest hundreds, thousands, and ten billions of transformation bodies."
He extensively established skillful means and further addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"Such Bodhisattvas, within Jambudvīpa in the Sahā world, employ hundreds of thousands of millions of skillful means to teach and transform beings. He further addressed Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"You must employ hundreds of thousands of skillful means to exhort these people. He also said: "By the power of skillful means, the Bodhisattva pulls them out from their fundamental karma."
[This is] the condition (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*), he causes them to attain liberation.
Kṣitigarbha himself says: "I too, by means of hundreds of thousands of skillful means, deliver such persons as these. Therefore, skillful means serves as the function of this present sutra.

In Sanskrit, it is *upāyakauśalya*; here it is translated as "skillful means" (*fangbian*). My ancestor, the Great Master Zhiyi, explained it through three meanings. The first is: "Method" (*fang*)...
"Fa" (法) means "Dharma"; "bian" (便) means "application. To skillfully apply all dharmas to benefit sentient beings according to their capacities is the second meaning.

Second, "fangbian" (方便) means "gate. A gate is so named because it can provide passage; it provides passage to that which is to be reached. Expedient means (*upāya*) and skillful strategies serve as the gateway to the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
That the ultimate reality is made manifest is due to the efficacy of expedient means. Third, "fang" (方) means "secret"; "bian" (便) means "subtle. Subtlety leads to...

The "method" (fang) is precisely the true secret. The first two interpretations are both not the intended meaning of this chapter; the latter interpretation alone is precisely the intended meaning of this chapter (text).
Alternatively, one may fully employ all three meanings, as for example in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where the Vaipulya was first opened.

Thus, Jingxi [Zhiyi] composed an interpretation that advances and retreats, allowing for the inclusion of the discourse on the secret of the "gate of accommodation and selection. Now, the Kṣitigarbha [Sūtra] also...

Nevertheless, although this work primarily expounds upon the profound and subtle discourse, it must also encompass the explanations of the various approaches (dvāra-dharma). Thus, the three types of exegesis are all fully provided, so that the general purport of the entire sutra may be summarized.

Why is this so? It is because the Great Being Kṣitigarbha, prior to aeons as numerous as motes of dust, manifested his body to teach and transform beings according to their capacities, skillfully adapting to them.
His application of the Dharma is uniquely appropriate; the revelation of ultimate reality is timely, and the provisional gates are accessible for entry, thereby inspiring the aspiration for Bodhi.

I focus the mind within the *ālaya-vijñāna* and illuminate the *tathāgatagarbha* within the mind of ignorance; this is the correct and wondrous mastery of the method, which is the true secret of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Furthermore, whether it be a single hair, a single drop, a single grain of sand, or a single speck of dust, I shall gradually deliver and liberate them, causing them to attain great benefit—just as those who raise a hand or bow their head, or gather grains of sand to form a stupa in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all open the door to the Small [Vehicle].

Excellent. What difference is there in their attainment of Buddhahood? Moreover, when the assembly gathers in the celestial palaces and the manifested bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are assembled, their number exceeds that of the sands of the Ganges.

Even Mañjuśrī cannot fathom them. How do those who have already perfected the Way of the Buddha differ from the manifested bodies under the tree? And as for those who still abide as Bodhisattvas—how are they different?
It is as if they have surged forth from within the earth; therefore, three explanations must be provided to encompass this fully.

Thus we know that when a Great Being emerges into the provisional realm to benefit sentient beings, they take the arousal of the bodhicitta as the cause, non-referential great compassion as the root, and the skillful means of non-attainment as the ultimate consummation.
If there is no skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, it is like attempting to rescue someone drowning without a boat; since they are difficult to extricate, one may sink along with them.
If there are skillful means, it is like using a boat to pull others from the water; both self and others attain salvation, the old and young rejoice together, and one rescues them throughout the day.
Like a precious moon traveling through the sky without dwelling, it delivers beings for billions of kalpas; like the shadow of a wild goose passing over water without lingering, it leaves no trace.

Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means (*upāya*), it assists in manifesting the primary truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, the means possess the merit of establishing the school, while the school possesses the power of manifesting the means.
Therefore, one knows that skillful means are the wondrous function of true compassion and salvation. For this reason, they are called "inconceivable means."
This constitutes its functional efficacy.
Fifth, regarding the judgment of the unsurpassed *amṛta* (ghee) as a teaching (*śāsana*): generally speaking, "teaching" is a term used in a broad sense;
anything that involves pointing out, distinguishing, or explaining is termed a "teaching. The *Sìjiào yì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: "In general terms, 'teaching'..."
To explain principles and transform beings is its essential meaning. It is called "teaching" (*śāsana*) because it can explain principles and transform the minds of beings.
There are three meanings to this transformation: first, transforming evil into good; second, transforming delusion into understanding; and third, transforming the ordinary into the holy.
Now, the Great Being Kṣitigarbha manifests within the six realms of existence, employing the four *siddhāntas* to respond to conditions amidst the four inexpressibles. Following...

The teaching is proclaimed through the opportune moment (*tathatā-pratibhāna*) to transform the minds of sentient beings; in its general outline, it does not exceed these three [aspects]. Therefore, the characteristics of the teachings are judged based upon these. Question:

The Great Master employs the "three illuminations" (*tri-avabhāsa*) of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra to open up the "level ground" (*píngdì*) into three stages, and further takes the "five flavors" (*pañca-rasa*) of the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra to correspond with the three illuminations of the *Avataṃsaka*.
These two sūtras and two meanings mutually complement one another to judge the holy teachings of a single lifetime. Together—

The five periods are enumerated as follows: first, the Avataṃsaka period (the name established based on the sūtra); second, the Deer Park period (the name established based on the location); third, the Vaipulya period (the name established based on the teaching); fourth, the Prajñā period;

and fifth, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka and Nirvāṇa periods (both names established based on the sūtras). Regarding the four periods preceding and following [the Vaipulya], the determination of their flavor is fixed.
Those that do not fall within the preceding or following periods are all subsumed under the Vaipulya category, such as the *Prabhāsa*, the *Śrīmālā*, and the *Mahā*... [text truncated].
The *Saṃyuktāgama*, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, and others are examples of this. Now, the *Kṣitigarbha-praṇidhāna-sūtra* also belongs to the third period, the time of the *Samatā* (Equivalence) teachings.
Why, then, is it classified as belonging to the *Sarpis-manda* (Clarified Butter) stage? Answer: There is evidence for this. According to the *Tongji* (Comprehensive Record), Master [Daoxuan] states:

"In the fifty-third year, the *Ren-shen* year (referring to the reign of King Mu of Zhou), the Buddha first went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and entered the three-month summer retreat. He dispatched Mañjuśrī to..."
At her mother’s residence, she briefly bowed in reverence to the Triple Gem. Upon hearing this, milk flowed spontaneously from Queen Māyā’s breasts, reaching directly into the Buddha’s mouth.
She then departed with Mañjuśrī for the Buddha’s location. The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

When the three months were nearly at an end and he was about to depart into *nirvāṇa*, Śakra fashioned a triple staircase of precious jewels. The Buddha took his leave of his mother before the great assembly.
[The Buddha] was escorted [to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven]. Upon returning below to the Jetavana, [the text] states: "This is from the *Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Sūtra*. Donghu remarked:

"According to the *Dharmacaryā-sūtra*, 'Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Thus we know that the preaching of the *Dharmacaryā* took place on the full moon of the eleventh month in the year Xinwei.

According to the *Ascension to the Trāyastriṃśa Sūtra*, after the three-month summer retreat, he knew that the preaching of the *Dharmacaryā* was concluded, and that very day he departed for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Based on this..."

When three months were nearly at an end, he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*. It was on the fourteenth day of the second month of this year that he descended to Jambudvīpa, and on the fifteenth day he entered *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "On the fifteenth day of the second month, he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*.
This present sūtra, however, records the time when the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother, and the assembly gathered as auspicious signs appeared.
The manifested bodies of Kṣitigarbha gathered and preached this; therefore, it is clear that this sutra stands after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

It does not belong to the "Ghee" (the highest stage); to which flavor, then, should it be assigned? Question: To categorize the sutras according to their chronological sequence is indeed highly authoritative.

However, when examining the text of the *Sūtra of Contemplation*, there is virtually no mention of "opening and revealing" (*kaikhen*) throughout its beginning or end. How, then, can it be equated with the two aforementioned sūtras in terms of their respective timing and essence? Answer:
The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) gathers in the great [teachings], while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* gathers up the remnants. That which was to be recorded has all been recorded.
Now, the Buddha ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three reasons: first, to preach the Dharma for his mother, thereby repaying the kindness of her nurturing and requiting her grace.
1. The virtue of his arduous toil is intended to encourage those of later generations who lack gratitude. 2.

It is to console the celestial deities who have departed, thereby repaying them for their protection during this lifetime, and to entrust them with the bhikṣus of the final age, charging them to guard these beings so that no demonic obstacles arise.

3. It is to entrust the beings of the six realms—who suffer in hardship and have no end in sight to their seeking liberation—to Kṣitigarbha, instructing him to protect them until the arrival of Maitreya.
This passage concerning the descent of Maitreya clearly demonstrates that our Buddha’s compassion extends even to the final kalpa.

Why, then, must there be further explicit texts before we can judge [the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] to belong to the "cream" (amṛta) stage? One should examine it by analogy with such works as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-nirdeśa-sūtra*;

then, all doubts will naturally subside. Question: According to Gushan’s judgment, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is classified within the "cream" stage based on its hearing of the "wondrous Lotus. How is this so?
The claim that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* shares the same teaching as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) seems to have some basis. Why, then, did Donghu criticize it, saying:
"The ultimate consummation of a single transformation lies in its revelation (*kaixian*). The subtlety of this revelation finds its merit in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

As for the other sutras, those that contain 'perfect' (*yuan*) explanations all represent the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) within the context of the four teachings of the Vaipulya period. Yet Guishan now wishes to equate the *Śūraṅgama* with the *Lotus Sutra*..."

It is like the flavor of the finest *mahā-mṛdvīkā* (clarified butter) produced from flowers. This is the *Acintya-sūtra*, which collects the teachings of the Vaipulya; yet it has lost the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—its pure unity and lack of admixture.
Now, observing that Kṣitigarbha preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, it truly belongs to the Vaipulya where the four teachings are discussed together.

If we now judge this by analogy with that [text], would there not be the same error as that of Mount Gushan? Answer: In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the guest and host engage in mutual inquiry and debate.

The passage concerning "the mind seeing [itself]" is truly the remainder of the critique and refutation found in the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras. Its subsequent clarification of the three aggregates and seven elements perfectly accords with the Prajñāpāramitā teaching on the sublation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Hearing the discourse on the "wondrous Lotus," it is certainly situated after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This represents the sense of being "subsequent" within the general classification of the five periods of the teaching; how could it be judged to be identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*? Donghu refutes this based on the meaning of the text.

Both are appropriate. Now, the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* is a teaching given at one time within the celestial palace; it guides beings according to their capacities by transcribing the words of its original past context.
This is analogous to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which transcribes the past expedient means. How could this be the same as the error of Gu shan [Zhiyuan], who confused the pure with the mixed?
If that were so, then even in the *Cīvaravastu* of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is said: "The Tathāgata will not remain for long; after these three months..."
Regarding the events at the time of Parinirvāṇa and after Nirvāṇa, why not judge them to be identical to the *tīraka* (cream-of-ghee)? He replied:
"This cannot be treated as an analogy, for the *pitakas* and the *vimalakīrti* (the Perfect) are fundamentally distinct.

Furthermore, the accounts of events after Nirvāṇa found within the *Āgamas* belong to the category of 'texts common to all five periods,' which can be subsumed under their respective original divisions. However, this present sutra is entirely devoid of such dual applicability."

How could that [previous teaching] be used to challenge this one? Therefore, we know that this present sutra definitively takes the revelation of the unsurpassed *amṛta* (the finest essence) as its pedagogical characteristic (*śāsanalakṣaṇa*).
